chunks: "A real capacitor is a series chain: the capacitance, a little resistance, ESR, and a little inductance, ESL, from its leads, body and the connections to it.
At low frequency the capacitive reactance dominates and the part looks like a capacitor, impedance falling as one over omega C.
At the self-resonant frequency, one over two pi root LC, the capacitive and inductive reactances cancel and the impedance bottoms out at the ESR.
Above that, the inductance dominates and the impedance climbs as omega L, so the capacitor has turned into an inductor.
That matters because the fast current a chip needs lives above resonance.
A 100 nanofarad capacitor with half a nanohenry resonates around 22 megahertz, and at 100 megahertz it's 0. 31 ohms, whatever its capacitance.
Increase the inductance to 3 nanohenries, with long traces and far vias, and resonance drops to 9 megahertz and the 100 megahertz impedance rises to 1. 9 ohms.
So parasitic inductance sets how fast the capacitor can respond, through L di/dt, limits its useful bandwidth, and, with other capacitors in parallel, creates anti-resonance peaks.
The total inductance includes the part's ESL, pads, vias and plane spreading, and the mounting is usually the bigger part.
That's why layout, not the capacitor value, decides performance at high frequency."
